passages.t: Gold grown dull: the city then and now
passages.happening:
The fourth poem opens with the cry of the first two: “How the gold has become tarnished, the pure gold has become dull!” (verse 1). The gems of the temple lie scattered on every street corner. ‘How the precious sons of Zion, once worth their weight in pure gold, are now esteemed as jars of clay’ (verse 2).

Even jackals nurse their young, the poet says, but his people have become cruel, like the ostrich in the wilderness (verse 3). Babies are parched with thirst. ‘Little children beg for bread, but no one gives them any’ (verse 4). People who once ate delicacies are destitute in the streets, and ‘those brought up in crimson huddle in ash heaps’ (verse 5).

‘The punishment of the daughter of my people is greater than that of Sodom’ (verse 6), which was overthrown in an instant. The nobles were once ‘brighter than snow, whiter than milk’ (verse 7). Now they are blacker than soot, and ‘they are not recognized in the streets’ (verse 8). Their skin has shriveled on their bones.

‘Those slain by the sword are better off than those who die of hunger’ (verse 9). Verse 10 returns to the worst thing the famine did, the curse already named in chapter 2. These notes name it and do not quote it. And the poet says, ‘The LORD has exhausted His wrath; He has poured out His fierce anger’ (verse 11). He has kindled a fire in Zion that has burned down to her foundations.
passages.hearers:
The siege had lasted about a year and a half, and the famine grew so severe that the people of the land had no food. The first hearers did not need these pictures explained. They had seen them.

The contrasts depend on what the ancient world valued. Gold was the most lasting of metals, thought to be beyond corruption. Clay pots were cheap and easily smashed. Healthy, well-fed skin was a sign of rank, and hunger showed on the body. So the nobles who had been fair and ruddy are now dark and shriveled, and nobody knows them.

The jackal and the ostrich were proverbs. Even the jackal nurses its young, while the ostrich was thought to leave its eggs in the sand. The poem says the siege had made parents unable to do what even wild animals do. It is not blaming the mothers. It is saying what famine does to people.

Sodom was the byword for a city destroyed. The poem says Jerusalem's punishment was greater, because Sodom fell in a moment while Jerusalem starved slowly. Verse 10 repeats one of the covenant curses of Deuteronomy 28, as chapter 2 did.

This poem is an acrostic too, but each stanza is two lines instead of three. It is shorter and quieter than chapters 1 and 2. It looks at the siege once more, as if the survivors had to see it again before they could move on.
passages.later: The ostrich of verse 3 is the bird of Job: ‘She treats her young harshly, as if not her own’ (Job 39:16). And Ezekiel compared Jerusalem with Sodom in the same way: ‘your sister Sodom and her daughters never did as you and your daughters have done’ (Ezekiel 16:48).
passages.hard:
Why is Jerusalem's punishment called greater than Sodom's, and how should a reader carry verse 10?

Sodom was the city destroyed in Genesis 19, proverbial for wickedness and sudden ruin. The poem says Jerusalem's punishment was greater (verse 6), not necessarily because her sin was worse in kind, but because her suffering was longer: Sodom was overthrown in an instant, and Jerusalem starved slowly. Some interpreters also see a principle stated elsewhere in Scripture, that more is asked of those who have been given more. Jerusalem had the law, the temple and the prophets, and so bore a heavier responsibility.

Verse 10 names what hunger drove people to in the siege. The poem does not linger, and it does not say that anyone deserved it. It is a cry of horror, not a lesson.

This is Judah's own Scripture, grieving Judah's own losses. It is not a key for reading anyone else's suffering, and it gives no one a warrant to say that any people's suffering, then or now, is a punishment they deserved.

A word for anyone who has lived through a flood, a storm or another disaster. Your loss was not a judgment on you. When Jesus was asked about people killed when a tower fell, he refused that reading of a disaster: “Do you think that they were more sinful than all the others living in Jerusalem? No, I tell you” (Luke 13:4-5). If you are carrying this, you need people more than explanations. Please talk to someone you trust, and the Find Help page has people you can call.
passages.asks: The poem looks at what was precious and is now treated as worthless. Ask what in your life, or in a community you love, has been treated that way. And ask whether you are able to look honestly at a loss more than once, without hurrying to move on.

passages.t: The sins of the prophets and the priests
passages.happening:
‘The kings of the earth did not believe, nor any people of the world, that an enemy or a foe could enter the gates of Jerusalem’ (verse 12). Nobody had thought the city could fall.

Then the poet says why it did. It was ‘for the sins of her prophets and the guilt of her priests, who shed the blood of the righteous in her midst’ (verse 13).

Now those same leaders wander. ‘They wandered blind in the streets, defiled by this blood’ (verse 14), so that no one dared to touch their clothes. People shouted at them to go away, calling them unclean and telling them not to touch anyone (verse 15). So they fled and wandered, and among the nations people said they could not stay there either.

‘The presence of the LORD has scattered them; He regards them no more’ (verse 16). The priests are given no honor, and the elders find no favor.
passages.hearers:
Many believed that Jerusalem could not fall because God's temple stood in it. The prophets had to argue against that belief for years. Verse 12 says the whole world shared it, and the whole world was wrong.

Verse 13 blames the leaders. Prophets and priests were meant to guard the covenant, teach the law and warn the people. Instead, the poem says, they shed innocent blood.

The cry of verse 15 is the cry the law required of a person with a skin disease, who had to warn others away by calling out that he was unclean. Now the people shout it at their own priests and prophets. The religious leaders have become outcasts, and even the nations do not want them.

The chapter is clear about where the failure began. Corruption at the top of a religious community brought ruin on the whole.
passages.later: Jeremiah had said the same before the fall: ‘For both prophet and priest are ungodly; even in My house I have found their wickedness’ (Jeremiah 23:11). The cry the people shout comes from the law for a person with a skin disease, who must ‘cover his mouth and cry out’ (Leviticus 13:45).
passages.asks: The poem blames leaders who shed innocent blood and misled the people. Ask how a community of faith should respond when its leaders fail, and whether yours would be willing to hear it. And ask whether you have ever trusted a place or a person as safe simply because God's name was on it.

passages.t: Watching for help that never came, and the king caught
passages.happening:
The voice changes to the survivors speaking together. Their eyes failed as they looked in vain for help. ‘We watched from our towers for a nation that could not save us’ (verse 17).

The enemy stalked them, so that they could not walk in their own streets. ‘Our end drew near, our time ran out’ (verse 18). ‘Those who chased us were swifter than the eagles in the sky’ (verse 19). They were pursued over the mountains and ambushed in the wilderness.

Then the hardest loss. ‘The LORD’s anointed, the breath of our life, was captured in their pits’ (verse 20). They had said that under his shadow they would live among the nations.
passages.hearers:
The nation that could not save them was Egypt. Judah had trusted Egyptian help when it rebelled. For a short time an Egyptian army did come near, and the Babylonians lifted the siege, but the Egyptians went home and the siege began again. Jeremiah had said they would.

The pursuit over the mountains and the ambush in the wilderness fit what happened when the wall was broken. King Zedekiah and his soldiers fled by night toward the Arabah and were overtaken in the plains of Jericho. Zedekiah was taken to the king of Babylon at Riblah, where his sons were killed in front of him and he was blinded. The poem does not tell that part, and these notes do not dwell on it.

The king is called ‘The LORD’s anointed’. The Hebrew word, mashiach, is the word behind Messiah. Kings and priests were anointed with oil when they were installed. Here it names Zedekiah, the reigning son of David, and his capture seemed to end the people's hope. To call him the breath of their life shows how much they had hung on him, and some scholars think it is a hope Jeremiah would not have shared.
passages.later: Jeremiah had warned that ‘Pharaoh’s army, which has marched out to help you, will go back to its own land of Egypt’ (Jeremiah 37:7). A psalm grieves over David's line in the same way: ‘You have spurned and rejected him; You are enraged by Your anointed one’ (Psalm 89:38). And Jeremiah promised another king: ‘I will raise up for David a righteous Branch’ (Jeremiah 23:5).
passages.asks: The survivors watched from their towers for help that could not save them. Ask what you watch for when you are in trouble, and whether it is able to save. And ask whom you have hung your hopes on in the way the people hung theirs on their king.

passages.t: Edom's cup, and Zion's punishment complete
passages.happening:
The poem ends with two short words to two daughters. To Edom: ‘So rejoice and be glad, O Daughter of Edom, you who dwell in the land of Uz’ (verse 21). The words are bitter. ‘Yet the cup will pass to you as well’ (verse 21), and Edom will be drunk and exposed.

To Zion: ‘O Daughter of Zion, your punishment is complete; He will not prolong your exile’ (verse 22). But God will punish Edom's iniquity and expose her sins.
passages.hearers:
Edom was Judah's neighbor to the southeast. The two nations traced their descent from the twin brothers Jacob and Esau, so the prophets call Edom Judah's brother. When Jerusalem fell, Edom rejoiced, and Obadiah and Psalm 137 say it helped the invaders and cut off those who fled. The land of Uz, Job's homeland, is here linked with Edom.

The cup is the prophets' familiar picture of God's judgment, handed to a nation to drink until it staggers. Jerusalem has drunk it. Now it passes on.

Verse 22 is the first time in the book that Zion is told her suffering has an end. Chapter 3 said the Lord would not cast off forever. Here the city herself hears it. The Hebrew word avon means both iniquity and the punishment that follows it, and it is used twice in this verse: Zion's is complete, and Edom's is coming.
passages.later: Isaiah takes up the same word of comfort: ‘proclaim to her that her forced labor has been completed; her iniquity has been pardoned’ (Isaiah 40:2). Obadiah condemns Edom for its part in the fall: ‘Because of the violence against your brother Jacob, you will be covered with shame’ (Obadiah 1:10). And Jeremiah names the cup Edom must drink (Jeremiah 49:12).
passages.hard:
Is this simply a wish for revenge on Edom?

The prophets repeatedly condemn Edom for its conduct when Jerusalem fell, gloating over a brother nation and handing over people who were running for their lives. The closing verses express the conviction that God's justice applies to all, and that those who rejoiced at another's ruin will answer for it. The poem hands that judgment to God, not to Judah.

Edom here is an ancient nation, named for what it did in 587 or 586 BC. These notes identify no people or nation of the present day with Edom, and the verse gives no one a warrant to wish ruin on any people now.
passages.asks: Zion hears that her punishment is complete. Ask how believing that judgment has an end could change the way you face a hard season. And ask whether you have rejoiced at someone else's ruin, as Edom did, and what that says about your own heart.
